I generally use the synthetics to tell me when it's time to start looking for important levels on the crosspairs it correlates with. If a synthetic is made up of 3 pairs, and one of those 3 is at a nice looking level, but the other 2 aren't and the synthetic isn't either -then it's "wait".

Dudu is no fan of RTM, that much is clear at this stage, but I wish him well with his preferred analysis style, if it's making him good, consistent money. That's all we're in this game for at the end of the day.

Personally, I love RTM-style analysis. Is it perfect? Is it a panacea? No, not at all. Especially since the markets seems to be getting harder and harder to read recently (or maybe that's just me). It does however remain a sound and effective model to form a basis for looking for levels.

When I want to take an entry, I want to do so from a level that has "orders" (I'm not sure this can be thought of in the literal sense, but it's a good analogy for referring to important buying/selling levels on the chart). A FL/FTR that was formed after taking out a key opposing level - well, it's just a very good place to look for orders. Of course FLs/FTRs themselves don't "move the market" - the only thing that moves the market is people actually hitting the market with active buying and selling.

I've been using this approach for over a year now, and know that it forms the nucleus of a very successful, accurate method of trading. There are of course many exceptions and nuances, which take a long time to learn, and even when you "know it all", you still face the even larger battle of controlling yourself and your emotions - a battle which I am still nowhere near winning.

When I fuck up, I know it's my own fault, and no-one else's. Sometimes I make a total misread, but most of the time I'm just self-sabotaging. There's nothing wrong with the RTM style, provided you realise it's not a set of literal rules which MUST BE OBEYED AT ALL TIMES. Nothing works like that in trading.

The reality is, you have to take some of this, some of that, put the pieces together. Which HTF levels are in play, the trend, style of movement, PA, FLs/FTRs, engulfs, key SR (PAZ boundary, QM etc), even a bit of volume profiling, and a huge amount of experience.

There are many ways to skin a cat. I like this method because it gives me precision to anticipate massive price turns within a few pips, if I do my homework correctly. I'm interested in RR, and % on the account. Number of pips gained, number of trades won etc are useless metrics. All that matters is the money going on your account, and the quicker the better

The end result is to get rich. However you get there is largely irrelevant. We're all going to have our preferred styles, and be extremely defensive about them, that's just human nature.

Do you mind telling me why would you look at that level? Because level wasn't respected as either Demand and Supply before?

Buying/selling symmetry levels are just clear places on the chart where you can see heavy buying/selling took place in the past. Very often, price will make a reaction upon returning to them.

If you want to sell for instance, it makes sense to look for levels on the chart where you can see evidence of strong selling in the past.

A QM, if you think about it, is just buying/selling symmetry followed by a FO. The "real" orders go in, price then FOs to stop out those with early entries and get some more people going the wrong way, it reverses and an engulf occurs, and then price returns to the "real" level where the first orders went in.

As it happens, that level on CJ gave only a very small reaction, which was to be expected really given the strength of the up move.

You can't just blindly fade and take FTB to every old FL on every lower timeframe. You have to put everything together in terms of the bigger picture, and learn when it's best to step aside instead of trying to fade, or indeed look for the quick continuation instead.
